title: Kickers: stream the situation, not the leg
hook: Kickers are the least predictable position in fantasy, and the kicker himself is the least important part of the prediction.
html:
Confidence: High (eight seasons, 4,200 kicker-weeks, always scored on a held-out season)

TL;DR

Kickers are the least predictable position in fantasy, and the kicker himself is the least important part of the prediction. Ranking kickers by their own scoring history barely beats guessing; what actually predicts kicker points is the situation — is his team favored, is the game in a dome, does his coach settle for field goals.

What actually predicts kicker points

We built a weekly kicker model the same way as the defense model: add ingredients one at a time, test each version only on seasons it never saw. The ingredients that carry weight are all about circumstance. Win probability matters most — winning teams kick. A dome adds most of a point; wind of 15+ mph takes about half a point away. And coaching identity is real: teams whose drives habitually stall into field-goal attempts feed their kicker, while great offenses actually starve theirs, because touchdowns mean one-point extra points instead of three-point field goals.

The kicker's own recent scoring, added on top of all that? Nothing. His history is nearly irrelevant once you know his situation.

The ceiling is low everywhere

The honest numbers, in rank correlation (how well the model's weekly ordering matched reality; 0 is random, 1 is perfect): ranking kickers by their own points per game scores .08 — barely above a coin flip. The full model reaches .19. That's a real improvement, and it's still only about half the defense model's .30. This is kickers are noise with the measurement attached: the position is streamable, but even the best streaming signal is a gentle tilt.

What to do with it

Draft your kicker with your last pick — every finding on this site agrees on that. In season, don't agonize between two comparable kickers; there is no analysis that resolves that choice. When you do switch, take the kicker whose team is favored, indoors if possible, with a coach who kicks. That's the whole edge, and pretending there's more would be fake precision. The weekly kicker board on this site is built from exactly these inputs.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/28-kicker-model.md

title: Pick your defense with one number: the opponent's total
hook: The best way to pick a defense each week is the opponent implied total — the score Vegas expects the offense your defense is facing to put up, worked out from the point spread and the over/under. Lower is better.
html:
Confidence: High (eight seasons of defense-weeks, always scored on a held-out season)

TL;DR

The best way to pick a defense each week is the opponent implied total — the score Vegas expects the offense your defense is facing to put up, worked out from the point spread and the over/under. Lower is better. In eight seasons of backtesting, that single number predicted weekly defense scoring better than everything else we tried combined.

What we tested

We built the model in steps and scored each step by rank correlation — how well its weekly ordering of defenses matched reality, where 0 is random and 1 is perfect. Ranking defenses by their own scoring average manages .13. The opponent implied total alone jumps to .30. Then everything else — opposing O-line quality, giveaway-prone opponents, the defense's own sack rate, home field, wind, even a backup QB starting — adds almost nothing, because the betting line already knows all of it. When a starting QB sits, the spread moves before our data ever sees the news. That gap from .13 to .30 is the whole streaming edge.

Yes, it counts sacks and pick-6s

A fair objection: surely some defenses just make more plays than others. Two answers. First, the model predicts full defense scoring — sacks, interceptions, fumble recoveries, defensive touchdowns, and the points-allowed bonus. Those plays aren't ignored; they're most of what we're predicting. Second, better defenses do exist, and Vegas already prices them: when a great defense takes the field, the opponent's total drops because the market knows it's good. The implied total isn't an alternative to measuring defense quality — it contains it, priced by people betting real money. Meanwhile a defense's own sack and interception rates swing so hard week to week that they barely predict their own next game.

How to use it

Rank defenses by opponent implied total, full stop — each Vegas point off the opponent's total is worth roughly +0.4 defense points. Don't pay for a name-brand defense on draft day; stream the slot all season. And keep expectations honest: defenses average about 5 points with a weekly swing of about 6, the noisiest slot in fantasy, so the model is a tilt, not a prophecy. The design follows subvertadown's published work, and for 2026 week 1 his two free picks and ours were identical. This model powers the weekly defense board on this site; the kicker model is its noisier sibling.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/27-dst-model.md

title: Matchups and weather are worth about a point, at best
hook: We tested whether team strength, defensive matchups, weather, and receiver-vs-cornerback data improve fantasy projections. Season-long: nothing helps — team quality changes too fast year to year.
html:
Confidence: High (24 seasons of games for the ratings, 36,000 player-weeks for the weekly tests)

TL;DR

We tested whether team strength, defensive matchups, weather, and receiver-vs-cornerback data improve fantasy projections. Season-long: nothing helps — team quality changes too fast year to year. Week to week: knowing the opponent is worth about one point at QB and RB and zero at WR, and the Vegas line already prices most of it before you ever check a matchup chart.

The season-long test

We built our own team ratings from 24 years of games; they track the Vegas point spreads closely, so they're doing their job. It doesn't matter. Nothing predicts a team's scoring next season better than its plain points per game last season, and even that is a loose guide. Adding team ratings to our projection model changed its accuracy by exactly nothing — a player's own production already carries his team's context.

Week to week: one point, mostly at QB

Across 36,246 player-weeks, the one genuine weekly upgrade was usage-based expected points — what a player's carries and targets should have scored. That's buy volume, not efficiency again at weekly scale. On top of that, opponent quality and the betting line add value only at QB — fittingly, the position our league streams. Between two comparable players, a matchup-based start/sit call is a coin flip with a one-point thumb on the scale.

Weather follows the same pattern. Wind is what bites: 15+ mph costs QBs almost two points and receivers about half a point, while cold alone is mild and running backs shrug it all off. The snow-game folklore, stated correctly: bad weather doesn't make RBs better, it makes everyone else worse. But adding weather to the model gained nothing, because by the time you see the forecast, the implied total — the score Vegas expects a team to put up — has already moved.

The WR-vs-cornerback report failed its own test

We tested the receiver-versus-cornerback idea three ways, including scoring a full week of a commercial matchup report against actual results. Their matchup grade had zero relationship with real scoring — their "bad matchup" receivers actually outscored their "good matchup" ones that week — and the best predictor on their own page was simply how many routes a receiver runs. A defense's supposedly weak left side doesn't even persist within a single season. Volume and recent form are signal; matchup talk is noise.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/26-team-environment.md

title: Our projections out-rank the draft board, except at RB
hook: We built a projection model that predicts each returning player's fantasy points per game for next season from his usage, age, touchdown luck, draft pedigree, and salary.
html:
Confidence: Medium-High (consistent on seasons the model never saw, but it's one model, not yet stress-tested)

TL;DR

We built a projection model that predicts each returning player's fantasy points per game for next season from his usage, age, touchdown luck, draft pedigree, and salary. Tested only on seasons it never saw, it ranks players better than the market's draft board at QB, WR, and TE. At RB the market still wins, so there we average the two.

Where the idea came from

The starting point is a 2012 Stanford class project that predicted running back seasons with a simple line fit on the previous year's yards and touchdowns. Its author listed everything the approach lacked — age, playing-time context, injuries, positions besides RB. That list became our to-do list. The result is one model per position, 16 inputs each, trained on 2,232 player-seasons, using ridge regression — a line-fitting method that resists over-trusting any single stat.

How well it ranks

We score a board by rank correlation: how well two rankings agree, where 0 is a coin flip and 1 is identical, always measured on a season the model was never trained on. Our model beats the ADP board by about +.09 at QB, +.11 at WR, and +.15 at TE. At RB the market wins — running back value is depth-chart and situation knowledge that drafters genuinely price well — and there, averaging the model's rank with ADP beats either one alone. So the practical rule is simple: trust the model at QB, WR, and TE; at RB, split the difference with the board.

What the model learned

Its habits are sensible. Touchdown luck regresses — except at RB, where goal-line work is a job that persists. Age costs backs and receivers the most. Changing teams costs everyone, most of all QBs. A league-mate's salary idea works: a player's share of his team's payroll at his position is the single strongest QB signal — the paid guy plays. And draft pedigree keeps predicting even two seasons into a career, because teams keep feeding their sunk costs.

What it can't do

No rookies — they have no NFL season to learn from, and need a separate model. No coach or scheme inputs, because no clean free data source exists. And it predicts points per game, not games played; availability is the injury model's job. This model powers the season-long board on this site.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/25-player-model.md

title: Knowing the players beats clever draft order 40 to 1
hook: We computed the perfect draft: if you knew exactly how every player's season would go, what is the best possible 15-round draft? Perfect foresight is worth about 685 extra points a season.
html:
Confidence: High (the numbers come from an exact search; the interpretation needs care — the oracle has information, not skill)

TL;DR

We computed the perfect draft: if you knew exactly how every player's season would go, what is the best possible 15-round draft? Perfect foresight is worth about 685 extra points a season. The gap between the best and worst sensible draft strategies is about 17 points by the same yardstick. Knowing which players will hit matters roughly forty times more than the order you draft positions in.

What we computed

For each of six seasons and every draft seat, we searched for the single best 15-round draft against a room of steady computer opponents — a true ceiling, not an estimate. The first surprise is what the ceiling looks like: even a perfect draft still loses about 4% of its weekly head-to-heads. Nothing removes variance from this game.

What perfect drafts look like

The oracle's habits mostly confirm what the other findings say from the ground. It opens with a running back 58% of the time, usually the season's actual #1 back — the top of the RB curve is real even with the answer key. It buys the season's actual best QB in rounds 1–3 in 69 of 72 drafts: the early-QB option is fairly priced because you don't know which QB will hit, but the right QB is a bargain. It almost never takes a tight end early, and always takes its kicker last.

The season, though, is won in rounds 4 through 8. That's where the oracle loads up on players who go at middle-round prices and finish as top-six backs and top-four receivers. The market's biggest pricing mistakes live in the middle rounds — in round 1 the oracle mostly agrees with the crowd. And the endgame is for lottery tickets: 83% of its final-round picks are players nobody drafted at all, the season's waiver-wire heroes bought in advance.

How to read this honestly

The 685 points are foresight, not achievable skill — no one knows which undrafted receiver breaks out. What transfers is the structure: back first, QB timing, cheap tight end, and the middle rounds as the place player judgment pays. The 17-point spread among realistic strategies restates an earlier finding: once you draft with basic discipline, sequencing cleverness is nearly used up. Any further edge has to come from evaluating players better, not ordering picks better.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/24-hindsight-optimal-drafts.md

title: Running backs run out faster, so take yours first
hook: Taking a running back before a receiver is right — but not for the reason people think. RBs aren't underpriced; the market charges the correct premium for them.
html:
Confidence: High (eight seasons of real results, plus a forced-swap test in the simulator)

TL;DR

Taking a running back before a receiver is right — but not for the reason people think. RBs aren't underpriced; the market charges the correct premium for them. The real edge is that RB value drains off the board about 45% faster than WR value, so even at fair prices, the order you buy in matters. Take the back first. The receiver will still be there three rounds later.

What the value curves say

We took eight seasons of results and asked what the market's #1, #5, #12 running back and wide receiver actually returned in points. Compared at the same position rank, the back wins: the top RB outscores the top WR by about 35 points a season, the twelfth-best back wins by about 11, and past rank 18 or so the gap disappears.

But compare at the same draft pick — the same price — and the premium vanishes. The market moves running backs up the board by almost exactly the right amount. There is no cheap position to exploit.

So why take the back first?

Because of the slope. Both positions are fairly priced, but RB value falls 45% faster with every step down the board. The receiver you skip now has a close cousin available three rounds later; the back you skip does not. We proved this in the simulator by running the same drafter twice with everything identical except one pick forced to RB instead of WR. Forcing the back in round 1 or 2 produced a small but real gain in all-play record (your record if you had played every team every week). By round 3 the gain was gone — the curves have already converged.

One myth worth killing: at the same price, RBs miss only about two-thirds of a game more per season than WRs. Early backs carry that tax easily. Late backs are the real trap — past the top twelve, the bad-RB outcome is worse than the bad-WR outcome, and the waiver wire restocks receivers better.

The fine print

This is standard scoring only; leagues that award points per catch shrink or even flip the premium. And it doesn't automatically crown RB-RB-RB: part of that plan's edge comes from our room drafting backs a few picks late. In a disciplined room the dogma fades while the take-the-back-first logic holds — even perfect hindsight drafts open with a running back only 58% of the time.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/23-early-rb-vs-wr.md

title: The waiver wire is worth about ten points a season
hook: We ran the same team through the same season twice — once allowed to use the waiver wire, once forbidden.
html:
Confidence: Medium-High (a clean controlled comparison, three drafting styles agree; a later audit suggests these numbers run a little low)

TL;DR

We ran the same team through the same season twice — once allowed to use the waiver wire, once forbidden. The wire was worth 5 to 12 points a season, roughly 1% of a team's total, and nearly all of it comes from patching quarterback and kicker. The wire is roster maintenance, not a strategy.

The experiment

Identical draft, identical opponents, identical schedule — the only difference was permission to make waiver claims. We ran it for three different drafting styles and all three agreed: about ten claims a season bought roughly a point apiece. For scale, the entire question of which round to draft your QB spans about four points of all-play; the whole waiver wire is worth a quarter of that.

Where the points come from

Breaking the gain down by lineup slot tells the story. QB and kicker gained under all three styles. RB and TE actually lost points under all three — claiming there just churned the bottom of the bench, and sometimes churned off someone better.

The reason is roster structure, not football smarts. You start one QB and one kicker and roster one or two of each, so when yours is hurt or on bye you have an actual hole, and the wire fills it. At RB and WR you carry five to eight bodies for five starting slots; a real hole almost never opens.

The pickups themselves say the same. A waiver QB scored 11.9 points a week while held, was kept nearly six weeks, and was cut quickly only 10% of the time — a real player. A waiver RB scored about 4 a week and was cut within two weeks 41% of the time. That's not a lottery ticket hitting; that's churn. It's why a drafted backup QB adds nothing — the wire plugs the same hole — and it matches the bench-stash null.

What to actually do

Don't plan a draft around the wire; depth you draft is not replaceable by depth you claim. Do go to the wire for a QB or kicker hole — that's where every point of the gain lives (the kicker part is mostly bye-week patching, which is fine, since kickers are noise anyway).

One honest asterisk

A later audit of our simulated managers caught two flaws — claims wasted on players already done for the year, and starting holes left unfilled — both of which make the wire look less valuable than it is. We're rerunning with the fixes. The headline number could grow some, but the shape — small overall, concentrated at QB and kicker — is exactly what the roster-structure mechanism predicts, and we expect it to hold.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/22-waiver-wire-reality.md

title: What a Friday injury tag is actually worth
hook: Out or Doubtful means he is not playing — the actual play rates are 0.1% and 1%, so treat both as zero. Questionable means 69% to play, and about 83% of his usual production when he does.
html:
Confidence: High (the play rates and the Questionable discount come from about a thousand real game weeks; the per-injury-type details are Medium)

TL;DR

Out or Doubtful means he is not playing — the actual play rates are 0.1% and 1%, so treat both as zero. Questionable means 69% to play, and about 83% of his usual production when he does. Once a player actually sits, the typical absence is two weeks, and a quarter never play again that season.

Reading the tag

We matched eight years of Friday injury reports against Sunday box scores. Doubtful is not really "doubtful" — it's Out with paperwork; Doubtful players suited up 1% of the time. Questionable is the only tag with real uncertainty: 69% to play overall, but position matters. Receivers and tight ends play about 75% of the time, running backs 68%, and quarterbacks just 47%. A Questionable QB is a genuine coin flip to take the field.

Starting the Questionable guy

When a Questionable player does play, he delivers about 83% of his normal output on average — but again the position matters more than the average. A Questionable QB who plays is essentially full price. A Questionable RB costs you about 10%, a WR about 20%, and a TE about 25%. Bench the tight end on any close call; start the quarterback.

Once he sits, how long is he gone?

We tracked 675 absences of fantasy-relevant players. The typical absence is two weeks, but the injury named on the first report changes the plan:

First-listed injuryTypical absenceNever returns that season
Hamstring2 weeks10%
Concussion1 week27%
Ankle2 weeks28%
Knee2 weeks28%
Foot3 weeks34%

Hamstrings come back — hold. Feet are the stealth season-enders. Concussions are usually short but occasionally very long. Absences also get worse as they drag: a player already out three-plus weeks ends up missing nearly five on average, and a third never return that year. One more thing to price in: the first game back runs 15–25% below normal, so ease him back in rather than starting him in a must-win on faith.

The fine print

Injury labels are coarse. "Knee" blends a sprain and a torn ACL, so the table understates the bad tail once real news says ligament. And "never returns" counts every reason a player stayed out — including benchings and cuts — which makes it the right number for roster planning but not a medical prognosis.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/21-injury-model.md

title: Backup QBs and TEs are a free choice; timing isn't
hook: Whether you spend a late pick on a backup quarterback or tight end genuinely doesn't matter.
html:
Confidence: High (for "it makes no difference" — 1,440 seasons per version and two different base drafters agree; the timing details are Medium)

TL;DR

Whether you spend a late pick on a backup quarterback or tight end genuinely doesn't matter. We forced teams to take one, and banned teams from taking one, and every version finished within a third of a point of the control. Two timing mistakes are real, though.

What we tested

We ran our simulated league with strategies forced to draft a second QB or second TE at round 10, 12, or 14 — and with strategies banned from drafting one at all. Each version played 1,440 seasons against an identical field, and we repeated the whole experiment with two different base drafting styles. Every version landed within about a third of a point of all-play (your record if you had played every team every week) of the control. Taking the backup costs nothing; skipping it costs nothing. That bench spot is yours to play with.

Why the pick is worthless even though the backup plays

The surprise is that the backup genuinely plays. On rosters frozen after the draft, a round-12 backup QB started about four weeks a season — byes, injuries, the odd week he looked better than the starter — and added around 23 points. That sounds like value.

It isn't, because the waiver wire sells the same ticket. Almost all of those starts come in weeks where your lineup slot would otherwise be empty, and an empty slot gets filled by a Tuesday claim just as well as by a draft pick. Our waiver study found the same thing from the other side: a waiver QB is the one pickup that reliably works. A drafted backup and a claimed one plug the same hole.

The timing mistakes that are real

If you do want a backup QB, take him around round 10; waiting until 12–14 was mildly but consistently bad, because by then the startable backups are gone and you're burning the pick. Don't double up either — backup TE in round 12 plus backup QB in 13 was the worst combination we tried. And the big one: pushing your starting TE to round 10 with no follow-up plan cost about a point and a half of all-play, the largest penalty in the whole experiment. Waiting on TE still works, but only if you then stream the position — playing whichever waiver TE has the best matchup each week — instead of riding one late pick.

One caveat: this is calibrated to our family's habits. A room that hoards QBs early would make late backups scarcer and could change the QB answer.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/20-second-qb-te.md

title: Bench RBs are lottery tickets that barely pay
hook: The theory says to stash running backs on your bench because they can become starters overnight, while bench receivers stay dead weight. The first half is true — and it's nearly worthless.
html:
Confidence: Medium-High (a clean test with a clear answer; the ticket math itself is solid)

TL;DR

The theory says to stash running backs on your bench because they can become starters overnight, while bench receivers stay dead weight. The first half is true — and it's nearly worthless. Tilting a bench toward RBs bought about one extra percent of championships, inside the noise.

The true half

We looked at every player drafted in roughly rounds 8 through 15 from 2020 through 2025. Bench RBs and bench WRs averaged the same number of startable weeks — about three — but the shape differs. A late RB turned into a starter for three or more consecutive weeks 21% of the time, versus 13% for WRs. The overnight-starter path is real, and it's RB-specific: when a starter goes down, his backup inherits a whole job at once.

Why it doesn't show up in the standings

We then ran our simulated league with one team tilting its bench picks toward RBs, another toward WRs, and one not tilting at all. The RB-tilted team gained about half a point of all-play (your record if you had played every team every week) and about one percent of titles — differences small enough to be chance.

Three reasons the lottery doesn't pay. The waiver wire sells the same tickets: when a starter goes down, his backup is usually claimable that Tuesday, so stashing mostly pre-pays for what waivers offer — the same conclusion as our handcuff finding. Bench spots also have a day job, bye-week coverage, where a WR body works exactly as well. And the tilt only moves picks in rounds 9–15, where every option is worth just a few points either way.

The one tactical takeaway for our league

We checked the simulator against our six real drafts and found one mismatch: our actual room goes on a running back frenzy in rounds 10–12, harder than the model does. So if you want lottery RBs, take them by round 9, before the run starts. Rounds 10–12 are then the cheapest time in our draft for TE and WR darts, because everyone else is looking the other way.

Verdict: let RB break ties for your last bench spots. Don't spend mid-round picks on the theory.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/19-bench-composition.md

title: "Injury-prone" is mostly a myth
hook: Being hurt this year barely predicts being hurt next year. Across more than 1,200 player-seasons, injury history explained about half a percent of who misses time next season — and at quarterback and wide receiver the ca…
html:
Confidence: Medium (the QB and WR result is solid; the tight end exception rests on only 24 repeat cases)

TL;DR

Being hurt this year barely predicts being hurt next year. Across more than 1,200 player-seasons, injury history explained about half a percent of who misses time next season — and at quarterback and wide receiver the carryover is exactly zero. The exceptions are tight ends and, more weakly, running backs.

What we measured

We counted the weeks each player was listed Out or Doubtful on the official NFL injury report from 2017 through 2025, then asked whether this year's missed time predicts next year's. For quarterbacks and receivers it doesn't — at all. Receivers who missed two or more weeks actually repeated slightly less often than the never-injured ones (23% vs 25%). That's what a true zero looks like: the noise falls on both sides.

Tight ends are the exception. A TE who missed two-plus weeks missed significant time again 38% of the time, versus 19% for healthy ones — double the rate. Running backs showed a weaker echo (30% vs 18%), shaky enough that we wouldn't build a draft rule on it. A plausible reason: the injuries that tend to recur — soft-tissue pulls, high-contact roles — concentrate at those positions.

We also checked whether injury history predicts production. It doesn't. Among players healthy enough to stay rosterable, missed weeks add nothing to predicting next year's points once you know this year's points.

What to do with it on draft day

Never discount a QB or WR for injury history. When someone at the table calls a receiver "made of glass," that's a buying opportunity — the discount in his price is real and the extra risk isn't. A modest discount on tight ends coming off multi-week injuries is defensible; a small one at running back, maybe.

The honest limits

Our data only covers players who made it back onto rosters. Someone whose injury ended his career, or wiped out his whole next season, has no next year to measure and drops out of the sample. So this finding is about the ordinary range — sprains, hamstrings, ankles — not Achilles tears. And "weeks listed Out" is a proxy that occasionally counts a player who was really benched, not hurt. Neither issue rescues the injury-prone label for QBs and receivers, but they're why we stop short of calling anyone risk-free.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/18-injury-prone-is-mostly-myth.md

title: Bet on targets, not on efficiency stats
hook: Two receivers score the same points per game; next year, bet on the one who had more passes thrown his way. Targets predict next season's scoring even after you account for this season's points.
html:
Confidence: High (the target signal was positive in seven of eight year-pairs, and the efficiency zeros had plenty of data behind them)

TL;DR

Two receivers score the same points per game; next year, bet on the one who had more passes thrown his way. Targets predict next season's scoring even after you account for this season's points. The efficiency stats people cite — yards after catch, catch rate — add nothing at all.

What we tested

We took every rosterable player from 2017 through 2025 and asked one specific question: once you already know how many points a player scored this year, does any other stat tell you something extra about next year? Most don't. Targets per game for wide receivers do — the effect was positive in seven of eight year-to-year comparisons. Carries per game for running backs showed a faint echo, too weak to bank on, and for tight ends there was nothing.

The efficiency side was a clean sweep of zeros. Yards after catch, catch rate, even catch rate adjusted for how deep the targets were: none added anything once points were known.

The twist worth understanding

Yards after catch is a real skill — the same players post good YAC year after year. It still doesn't help you, because that skill is already baked into the points you can see. A stat can be stable and useless at the same time. You're not asking "is this player good"; you're asking "is he better than his points say," and YAC can't answer that. Targets can.

Why targets specifically

Our league is standard scoring — a catch earns nothing by itself — so a receiver who piles up targets without big plays looks worse than he is. His points understate his opportunity, and opportunity is what carries over. Points built on nine targets a game repeat; points built on a couple of long touchdowns don't. It's the same logic as the touchdown-luck finding: bet on what persists, fade what doesn't.

Names for this draft

Volume buys — receivers whose 2025 targets outran their points: Ja'Marr Chase, Justin Jefferson (also the biggest touchdown-luck buy, so he's flagged twice), Chris Olave, CeeDee Lamb, Amon-Ra St. Brown. Efficiency fades — points outran their volume: Christian Watson, Alec Pierce, Tee Higgins (also flagged twice, as TD-lucky), Jameson Williams.

One caveat: efficiency still matters when you're judging whether a player keeps his targets. It just deserves no extra weight on draft day when production is equal.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/17-buy-targets-not-efficiency.md

title: Last year's touchdown luck doesn't carry over
hook: Touchdowns are the flukiest stat in football, and drafters keep paying full price for them.
html:
Confidence: High (the effect showed up in all eight year-to-year comparisons we checked)

TL;DR

Touchdowns are the flukiest stat in football, and drafters keep paying full price for them. Players who scored more touchdowns than their chances deserved score about 1.6 points a game less the next season than equally productive players who got unlucky. Fade last year's TD-lucky players and buy the TD-unlucky ones.

Separating luck from skill

For every carry and every target, play-by-play data can estimate how likely a touchdown was — a target at the two-yard line is usually a score, a checkdown at midfield almost never is. Add those chances up and you get a player's expected touchdowns. The gap between actual and expected is, roughly, his touchdown luck.

Then the test: does beating your expected touchdowns one year predict beating them again the next? Across nine seasons of rosterable players, no — the carryover is statistically zero. But touchdowns are about 40% of standard scoring, so a lucky year inflates a player's points, his final ranking, and his draft price.

What that's worth

Take two players with the same points per game, one TD-lucky and one TD-unlucky. Next season the lucky one scores about 1.6 points a game less — roughly 23 points over our 14-week season, hiding in plain sight. That gap was negative in every one of the eight year-pairs we checked. QB passing touchdowns show the same pattern at the same size, but on a smaller sample, so treat that as supporting evidence rather than proof.

CeeDee Lamb38buy
Christian McCaffrey1721buy

"Fade" means don't pay the touchdown-inflated price, not never roster. These are one-to-two-points-a-game nudges — they don't override a changed role, age, or injury.

Where this could go wrong

Expected touchdowns come from a model, and a model can be wrong about specific players — a true goal-line hammer might beat his number year after year. Zero carryover means such players are rare, but check the usage before fading a repeat offender. And Jefferson's quiet 2025 had other causes too; still, he's the top buy here and in our targets finding, which is exactly why we like him.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/16-td-luck-regresses.md

title: A hot finish to the season predicts nothing
hook: "He finished the year on fire" tells you nothing about next season. A player's last few weeks predict next year worse than his full season does, and add nothing once you know his season average.
html:
Confidence: High (about a thousand player-seasons, and the answer is a firm, well-measured zero)

TL;DR

"He finished the year on fire" tells you nothing about next season. A player's last few weeks predict next year worse than his full season does, and add nothing once you know his season average. The kill shot: the last five weeks of a season are no more predictive than the first five weeks of the same season.

What we tested

For every offseason from 2017 through 2025, and every rosterable player, we asked what predicts next season's scoring better: the full season, or just the finish. About a thousand player-season pairs, scored under our league's exact settings. We measured with correlation, which is just a score for how well one number predicts another — 0 means no connection, 1 means perfect.

What we found

Full-season points per game predicts next season at roughly .5 to .6 depending on position. Every shorter window does worse: the last five weeks, the last three, and the final game predict progressively less, at every position. And once you already know a player's full-season average, adding "how he finished" improves the forecast by essentially nothing — the extra signal measures +0.04, which is statistically indistinguishable from zero.

The cleanest test compared the last five weeks of a season against the first five weeks of the same season. They predict next year equally well. December games feel more meaningful than September games; they aren't. A hot finish is a small sample wearing a story.

The one flicker

Running backs are the lone spot where the tail end might carry a whisper of extra signal — a back who takes over a backfield in December sometimes really does own the job going forward. The evidence is suggestive but didn't survive our stricter checks, so treat it as a tiebreaker at most, and only when the role visibly changed (the starter was traded or benched), not when a backup was merely hot.

Draft rule

Draft off full-season and multi-season rates. When an August ranking or a family member cites "the way he closed the year," that information is either already inside his season average or it's noise. This pairs with touchdown luck regressing: recent, vivid, story-shaped stats are exactly the ones to distrust.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/15-late-season-momentum-myth.md

title: Take your first quarterback in rounds 4 to 6
hook: We ran eight computer drafters that were identical except for one thing: the earliest round they'd take a quarterback.
html:
Confidence: Medium-High (clean apples-to-apples design; trust the shape of the curve more than any single number)

TL;DR

We ran eight computer drafters that were identical except for one thing: the earliest round they'd take a quarterback. Rounds 4–6 came out on top, anywhere from round 2 to 8 was nearly as good, and the real mistake was waiting past round 10. Our family's actual habit — first QB around round 5 — turns out to be exactly right.

The experiment

Comparing quarterback strategies across different leagues and seasons muddies everything, so we changed exactly one dial. Eight copies of the same disciplined drafter, each banned from taking a QB before a target round — round 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, or 12 — and otherwise identical, each drafted through 720 simulated seasons in a room modeled on our family's real drafts.

The curve

Earliest QB roundAll-play record
2.578
3.579
4.582
5.588
6.587
8.575
10.564
12.549

All-play is your record if you had played every team every week — the least lucky way to score a season. The whole spread is about 4 points of all-play, roughly half a win a year, with one clear peak at rounds 5–6. Reaching up to round 2 costs about 1 point; waiting until round 12 costs about 4. The penalty for too early is mild; the penalty for too late is the real one.

Why the middle wins

The top quarterbacks are genuinely better, but the worst starting QB in a 12-team league still scores around 16 points a game — the position has a high floor. Spend a round-2 pick on one and you've skipped a running back or receiver, positions with no such floor (finding 01). Wait past round 10 and you're choosing from the bottom of the startable barrel, and the waiver wire can't rescue you at quarterback (finding 06). Rounds 4–6 is where a top-ten quarterback naturally drifts to in our league's draft rooms.

Fine print

"Round 5" means the drafter opens its window there; the actual pick usually lands somewhere in rounds 5–7 depending on the room. And all eight of these drafters beat the family-modeled bots by a wide margin regardless of QB plan — but that gap is about disciplined drafting in general (finding 03), not about quarterbacks. Don't read it as a QB effect.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/14-qb-round-sweep.md

title: Handcuff running backs: real insurance, zero edge
hook: Drafting your starting running back's backup — his "handcuff" — really does pay out: about 9.5 points a game in exactly the weeks your starter sits.
html:
Confidence: Medium-High (1,440 simulated seasons put the effect at almost exactly zero — a precise tie, not a shrug)

TL;DR

Drafting your starting running back's backup — his "handcuff" — really does pay out: about 9.5 points a game in exactly the weeks your starter sits. But a drafter who pays extra to own his handcuffs finishes in a dead tie with one who doesn't, because the insurance is worth exactly what the picks it costs are worth. Take a handcuff on a coin flip; never reach for one.

The insurance is real

We found 124 starter-and-backup pairs over six seasons. When the starter missed a week, the handcuff averaged 9.5 points a game — right at low-end RB1 level — and hit that level in about half the outage weeks. When the starter played, the same backup averaged 4.6, below what the waiver wire offers. That's a nearly pure insurance policy: worthless in good times, valuable in exactly the bad ones. The 2025 case that prompted the question behaved to spec — Rachaad White gave 7.7 points a game during Bucky Irving's eight missed weeks, versus 3.6 the rest of the time.

But it buys no wins

We put two identical computer drafters into our simulated league — same behavior in every way, except one pays a premium from the middle rounds onward to grab the backups of its own running backs. Across 1,440 simulated seasons they finished in a statistical dead heat: .599 versus .598 all-play (all-play = your record if you had played every team every week). That's not "we couldn't detect a difference." The difference is measured tightly, and it's zero.

Why it cancels out

A bench spot is a bet on the future, and the two bets pay the same. The handcuff is a narrow bet: it pays only if your starter goes down, and even then only the gap between him and your next-best fill-in. The best-available player is a broad bet: he pays on any bye week, any injury at his position, or just by outscoring your flex some week. Narrow-but-big and broad-but-small come out even. And when a starter does go down, the whole league can see the promoted backup on waivers — owning him in advance is less exclusive than it feels.

The rule

If your guy's backup and someone else's player are a genuine coin flip in round 10, take yours — the insurance is free at that price, and you'll set your lineup with less stress. Just never spend a round early to get him. You're not buying an edge; you're buying a feeling.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/13-handcuffs-are-free-insurance.md

title: Two straight finals losses are bad luck, not a broken plan
hook: The Jackels were the best regular-season team in the league two years running — 24-4 combined, 1 seed and most points scored both years — and lost the championship game both times. That's not a broken process.
html:
Confidence: High (simulation math plus the league's own record book)

TL;DR

The Jackels were the best regular-season team in the league two years running — 24-4 combined, #1 seed and most points scored both years — and lost the championship game both times. That's not a broken process. A title comes down to two single-week coin flips, and even a dominant roster only tilts those flips.

What actually happened

2024: 13-1, the most points in the league by 160, the #1 seed — and a loss in the final to the Bombers, who had the #3 draft haul. 2025: 11-3, most points again, #1 seed again — and a loss in the final to the Bullies, who went 7-6 in the regular season and had the seventh-best draft. The league's two best drafting seasons (we checked) produced two silver medals.

The math of a short bracket

Weekly dominance compounds much more weakly than it feels like it should. Suppose a team is good enough to beat an average playoff opponent 65% of the time — a huge weekly edge. Even with a first-round bye, the title takes two straight wins, and 65% twice is only about 42%. Play two seasons at that level and you'll lose at least one of the two finals more often than not.

The simulator says the same thing from the other direction: the best draft strategy we've ever tested wins the championship about 20% of the time (finding 01). That's roughly two and a half times a team's fair share in a 12-team league — and it still means that four seasons out of five, the best plan in the room does not win the ring.

What the league should take from this

The tempting lesson after any season is "copy the champion." But in both years the champion drafted worse than the runner-up. Titles identify the luckiest good-enough team, not the best process. If you want to judge process, look at all-play record — your record if you had played every team every week, which strips out schedule luck — and total points. By those measures, one team has been the best in the league two years running.

None of this means the playoffs are pure luck. A dominant team really does win far more titles over time. It means two specific finals are far too small a sample to indict anything.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/12-championship-variance.md

title: Auditing the Jackels: strong drafts, two repeat leaks
hook: We graded the Methuen Jackels' drafts against all 12 teams. The 2024 haul was the best in the league, 2025 was fourth, and a perfect-hindsight redraft keeps most of the actual picks.
html:
Confidence: High (it's our league's own data, fully counted)

TL;DR

We graded the Methuen Jackels' drafts against all 12 teams. The 2024 haul was the best in the league, 2025 was fourth, and a perfect-hindsight redraft keeps most of the actual picks. The two real leaks, each committed twice: paying a premium for a tight end, and buying a "discounted" veteran receiver in rounds 4–5.

How we graded

You can't judge a draft by the final standings — waivers, lineup calls, and luck pile on top. So we scored every team's drafted roster only: the points it would have produced with a perfect lineup set every week. Nobody manages perfectly, but the same generous yardstick applied to all 12 teams makes the ranking fair.

The good news

The 2024 Jackels draft produced 1,779 perfect-lineup points — first of 12 teams — with Derrick Henry, Josh Jacobs, and Terry McLaurin all arriving well below their market price. Patience, not reaching. The 2025 draft came in fourth, and most of the gap back to 2024 was three injuries (Tyreek Hill, Bucky Irving, Najee Harris) erasing about 140 expected points.

We also replayed each draft with perfect knowledge of the season: at every Jackels pick, take the best player still on the board. The striking part isn't the score (the real 2024 draft captured 81% of that impossible ceiling) — it's that the all-knowing version keeps most of the actual picks. The player identification is close to optimal. The remaining gap concentrates in two habits.

The two leaks

Leak20242025
Premium tight endKincaid (rd 8) → TE27LaPorta (rd 6) → TE24
Discount veteran WR, rds 4–5Cooper → 74 ptsTyreek → 30 pts

Both are patterns we've since tested league-wide. Paying up at tight end doesn't work (finding 05) — nearly-free tight ends outscored both picks. And the fallen star at a discount is the worst-performing discount type we've measured (finding 09). Across two years the leaks cost roughly a full top-20 receiver season's worth of points.

The elephant

Best draft in the league, 24-4 across two seasons, two #1 seeds — and two runner-up finishes. That's not a hidden third leak; it's what playoffs do to the best team, and it gets its own write-up (finding 12). Worth noting: in both years the eventual champion drafted worse than we did, with the #3 and #7 hauls.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/11-methuen-jackels-audit.md

title: The WR age cliff is real, but smaller than it looked
hook: Our first pass found a tidy rule: mid-round receivers aged 29–30 are a death zone, and 31-plus veterans bounce back. We stress-tested it and only half survived.
html:
Confidence: Low-Medium (half the original story died under stress-testing; read this one as a lesson in method too)

TL;DR

Our first pass found a tidy rule: mid-round receivers aged 29–30 are a death zone, and 31-plus veterans bounce back. We stress-tested it and only half survived. Older receivers really do underperform, with 29–30 the worst ages in most versions of the test — but the 31-plus rebound was noise. Use age as a tiebreaker, not a rule.

The version that was too good

Slicing six years of mid-round receivers by age gave a striking picture: 29- and 30-year-olds hit (finished top-24) only 17% of the time and busted 61%, while every other age group busted somewhere between 33% and 45%. Better still, receivers 31 and older seemed to bounce back. It came with a neat story — the market panics about age at the wrong moment — and a ready-made draft rule. Which is exactly when you should get suspicious.

How we tried to break it

The danger with a result like this is called overfitting: slice 200 player-seasons into enough age buckets and one bucket will look extreme by pure chance — and then your brain invents a story for it. The cure is to change things that shouldn't matter and see whether the pattern survives: split the years in half, widen and narrow the draft-price range, move the definition of a bust.

The 29–30 slump passed most of those checks. It shows up in six of seven versions of the test, in both halves of the data. But one reasonable slice — looking only at the middle of the mid-round range — erased it entirely. And the 31-plus rebound failed outright: it flips direction depending on which years you look at, and the whole "rebound" is a handful of specific players (Davante Adams twice, Diggs, Keenan Allen, Hopkins) having good recent seasons.

What we actually believe now

Receivers 29 and older underperforming as a group: probably real, size uncertain. The 31-plus bounce-back: no claim should rest on it. The practical version: between two otherwise-equal mid-round receivers, lean younger — and let the sturdier filters make the real decision. Buy discounts that come from a bad situation (finding 08); don't buy discounts that come from the player's own collapse (finding 09).

We're publishing the broken half on purpose. A site that only showed findings that survived would quietly teach you that every tidy pattern is trustworthy. Most aren't.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/10-wr-age-effects.md

title: The bounce-back discount receiver is usually a trap
hook: The "he was great two years ago, he'll bounce back" pick is usually a trap. Mid-round wide receivers coming off a collapse year busted 53% of the time — clearly worse than ordinary mid-round picks — and youth didn't save…
html:
Confidence: Medium (only 17 players fit the profile, but the pattern held in every slice we cut)

TL;DR

The "he was great two years ago, he'll bounce back" pick is usually a trap. Mid-round wide receivers coming off a collapse year busted 53% of the time — clearly worse than ordinary mid-round picks — and youth didn't save them. A cheap price on a former star usually means the market knows something, not that it missed something.

Who we mean

Every draft board has a few receivers with the same résumé: a top-20 wide receiver two seasons ago, a collapse last season, and now a friendly mid-round price. The pitch writes itself — "you're getting the old version at a discount." We pulled every mid-round WR from the last six drafts who fit that exact profile: 17 players, from DeAndre Hopkins to Kenny Golladay.

What we found

They busted 53% of the time, versus 42% for all other mid-round receivers, and on average they finished about 24 ranking spots below their draft price — nine spots worse than the ordinary mid-rounder. Age didn't rescue anyone: the under-29 group busted 56% and the 29-and-over group 50%. And the misses weren't near-misses. They were total zeroes — the Golladay and DJ Chark seasons you cut by October.

Why the market gets this one right

A collapse usually has a cause that sticks around: fading speed, a broken offense, a younger teammate who took the job. The discount isn't the market missing something — it's the market knowing something. The trap feels profitable because of selective memory: everyone remembers Tee Higgins bouncing back, nobody remembers the nine guys who didn't.

There's a cleaner rule hiding here. A mid-round discount is worth buying when it comes from the player's situation — a good receiver stuck on a bad team really does pay off (finding 08) — and not worth buying when it comes from the player's own play. It's also a different question from plain age discounts, which turned out murkier than we hoped (finding 10).

Where this could go wrong

Seventeen players is a small group, so the exact gap could shift as seasons get added — that's why this is Medium confidence, not High. And the few who did bounce back (Diggs, Keenan Allen, Higgins) share a tell: they kept a big share of their team's targets even during the down year. Volume surviving the collapse may be the real signal, and it's the first thing we'll test when next season's data lands. We've paid this tax ourselves, twice — see the audit of our own drafts.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/09-decline-discount-trap.md

title: In the mid rounds, draft the top receiver on a bad team
hook: In the middle rounds, target a team's clear 1 receiver on a team coming off a losing season.
html:
Confidence: Medium (a clear effect, but from 47 players in one six-year window)

TL;DR

In the middle rounds, target a team's clear #1 receiver on a team coming off a losing season. From 2020 to 2025, those receivers finished in the top 24 at their position 43% of the time, versus 25% for mid-round receivers with neither trait — nearly double the hit rate. Bad teams still throw to somebody.

Who hits and who busts

We took every receiver drafted in roughly rounds 4 through 10 over six seasons — about 200 players — and sorted them by two traits: was he his team's top receiver, and was his team coming off a losing year? The group with both traits hit top-24 at 43%. The group with neither hit at 25%. Worth knowing: mid-round receivers as a whole underperform what they cost, so this is less "free money" and more "the only group that comes close to earning its price."

The surprising flip side: #1 receivers on good teams busted most often of all, at 46%. Those tend to be aging veterans whose price rests on reputation — the pattern we chase down in the decline-discount trap.

Why it works

Bad teams spend their Sundays trailing, and trailing teams throw. The clear top receiver soaks up those targets, and standard scoring pays yardage — which garbage time supplies for free. Meanwhile the market discounts the whole roster because the team is bad, so the one player the offense actually runs through goes a few rounds too late.

We've cashed this ticket twice. McLaurin in 2024 went as the 32nd receiver drafted and finished #5. Olave in 2025 went 34th and finished #6. Both were the clear top target on a team nobody believed in.

Treat it as a lean, not a law

Two honest limits. The headline group is only 47 players, so the gap, while large, is measured loosely — and we noticed the pattern after seeing picks like McLaurin work, so the real test is whether it keeps working in future seasons. And this is about who to pick within rounds 5 through 9. It is not a reason to spend more early picks on receivers — that still loses.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/08-bad-team-wr1-edge.md

title: How fast each position falls off a cliff
hook: We averaged six seasons of points per game at every rank of every position. Running back value falls off a cliff, receivers stay nearly flat for twenty ranks, tight end is elite-or-nothing, quarterbacks score the most bu…
html:
Confidence: High (plain averages over six full seasons)

TL;DR

We averaged six seasons of points per game at every rank of every position. Running back value falls off a cliff, receivers stay nearly flat for twenty ranks, tight end is elite-or-nothing, quarterbacks score the most but the last starter is still fine, and kickers are a rounding error. Every draft rule on this site comes from this one table.

The table

Points per game by positional rank, 2020–2025, our league's scoring:

RankQBRBWRTEK
#123.519.115.711.211.5
#420.815.112.48.210.0
#1017.812.310.66.19.1
#1615.511.09.55.18.4
#2811.98.68.03.67.1

In our lineup — 1 QB, 2 RB, 2 WR, 1 TE, an RB/WR flex, and a kicker across 12 teams — the "last starter" is roughly QB12, RB30, WR30, TE12, and K12.

How to read it

Running back is the cliff: the #1 back outscores the #10 by almost 7 points a game, and the position's entire premium lives in the first dozen names. That's the engine behind opening RB-RB-RB.

Receivers are the opposite — the #7 wideout outscores the #28 by only 3.5 points a game. Mid receivers are nearly interchangeable, which is why WR-heavy drafting fails and why the mid-round WR game is about picking the right ones, not picking them earlier.

Tight end drops from a genuine weapon at #1 to barely-above-the-worst by #7, so pay elite or pay nothing. Quarterback has the biggest total drop, but the twelfth starter still scores more than any RB2 — a high floor that makes waiting survivable. And three points separate the best kicker from the worst starter, the smallest gap on the board (and you can't predict it anyway).

One caution

These are end-of-season ranks, which is hindsight — nobody knew in August which back would be #1. A draft-day version of the chart is noisier but the same shape. And averaging six seasons smooths real year-to-year swings; the strategy backtests, not this chart, carry the risk story.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/07-what-a-starter-is-worth.md

title: Pay for a QB if you like — never plan to stream one
hook: Expensive quarterbacks are worth it — they're just not a bargain. Taking one early neither helps nor hurts in our league.
html:
Confidence: Medium-High (the sim and the raw numbers agree; the effects are moderate rather than huge)

TL;DR

Expensive quarterbacks are worth it — they're just not a bargain. Taking one early neither helps nor hurts in our league. What hurts is waiting past round 10 and planning to live off the waiver wire: that plan cost about 3 points of all-play, because most years the wire holds no good quarterbacks at all.

What the market gets right

Quarterback has the biggest point gap of any position: the guys drafted early average around 21 points a game, and the ones drafted late around 13. So paying up buys real points. But the draft already knows this — in simulation, a team that grabs an elite QB early finished at .592 all-play (your record if you played every team every week), essentially identical to the .591 of a team with no quarterback opinion at all. You get what you pay for, exactly.

What actually costs you

The team that banned quarterbacks before round 10 and planned to stream replacements finished at .563 — roughly 3 points worse. The reason is supply. In two of the last six seasons, zero waiver-wire quarterbacks finished in the rest-of-season top 8, and the rare hits were only obvious in hindsight. With twelve teams rostering about 24 quarterbacks, essentially every startable passer is already owned.

The hindsight test

We also ran drafts where an oracle knows how the season turns out. In 69 of 72 of those perfect drafts, the oracle takes the season's actual best quarterback in round 2 or 3 — the right QB is a bargain every single year. "Fairly priced" just means nobody knows which one he is in August. (Our round-by-round sweep puts the sweet spot at rounds 4–6.)

The rule we'd actually use

Don't reach for the first quarterback off the board. But when a top-6 guy is still sitting there in rounds 3 through 6 — Josh Allen at pick 30 in our 2024 draft, who finished as the QB2 — take him, and never leave the draft planning to stream the position. One caveat: our league scores 4 points per passing touchdown. At 6 points, paying up early would probably become a genuine edge, not just a fair trade.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/06-qb-timing.md

title: Wait on tight end: round 10 or later
hook: Every season, half or more of the year's top-8 tight ends cost a round-8-or-later pick — or nothing at all. So never spend an early pick on one.
html:
Confidence: High (for "don't pay up" — the data, the sim, and our own drafts all agree; the newer "wire is drying up" wrinkle is Medium)

TL;DR

Every season, half or more of the year's top-8 tight ends cost a round-8-or-later pick — or nothing at all. So never spend an early pick on one. One update, though: the extreme version — draft no tight end and live off free agents — is quietly drying up. Take yours in round 10 or later, and hit the wire only if he busts.

The pattern, six years running

We tagged every top-8 tight end from 2020 through 2025 with what he cost on draft day. The lists are full of players who were nearly free: Taysom Hill, Robert Tonyan, and Jonnu Smith were undrafted in their top-8 years, and in 2025 three of the top eight went at pick 140 or later. The players who cost round-2-through-6 picks show up too — but not often enough to justify the price.

The shift worth knowing: undrafted tight ends cracking the top-8 went 3, 2, 3 in 2020–22, then 0, 1, 0 in 2023–25. The league-wide habit of drafting deep sleeper tight ends seems to have thinned the free pile. That's only three seasons of evidence, so we hold it loosely — but it's why the advice is "round 10," not "never draft one."

Our own receipts

We've paid the premium ourselves. Kincaid at pick 91 in 2024 finished as the TE27. LaPorta at pick 62 in 2025 finished TE24. Two premium prices, two scrub outcomes — while Jonnu Smith and Goedert, who cost nearly nothing, both outscored them by 50-plus points. (More of our own draft grades in the audit.)

Why the middle of the position is worthless

The value curves explain it: the 7th-best tight end scores about 6.9 points a game and the 12th about 5.8. Beyond the top few names, everyone's tight end is roughly the same guy, so a mid-round pick buys you almost nothing over a late one. A true elite — Kelce in 2020, McBride in 2025 — is genuinely valuable. The claim isn't that tight ends don't matter; it's that the price the league sells them at hasn't been worth paying in six years of trying.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/05-never-pay-up-for-te.md

title: A hot start tells you nothing about a kicker
hook: The top-scoring kicker after week 1 finished the rest of the season around 19th out of 34 kickers — the middle of the pack — and even the best kicker through four weeks rarely stayed on top.
html:
Confidence: High (every kicker, every week, six straight seasons)

TL;DR

The top-scoring kicker after week 1 finished the rest of the season around 19th out of 34 kickers — the middle of the pack — and even the best kicker through four weeks rarely stayed on top. Draft any kicker with your last pick, swap for bye weeks, and never spend a waiver claim chasing last week's hero.

What we checked

We took every kicker with weekly stats from 2020 through 2025 and asked one question: does a hot start predict the rest of the season? Here's the best kicker through the first four weeks of each year, and where he ranked from that point on.

YearHot kicker (wks 1–4)Rest-of-season rank
2020Stephen Gostkowski#26
2021Justin Tucker#10
2022Younghoe Koo#23
2023Jake Elliott#19
2024Brandon Aubrey#8
2025Spencer Shraderlost the job

The full picture — every kicker's early rank plotted against his finish — is a shotgun blast with no pattern in it. And 2025's week-1 hero, Shrader, didn't even stay employed long enough to qualify.

Even if you could predict it, the prize is tiny

The gap between the best startable kicker and the worst is about 3 points per game — the smallest spread of any position on the roster (the value curves make this concrete). So kicker is broken in both directions: you can't identify the good one in advance, and even a perfect guess is worth a field goal a week.

To be clear, kickers do score. The top kicker averaged 11.5 points a game, more than the top tight end. The claim isn't that the position is worthless — it's that no early pick or waiver move can select the good one, so paying anything for the attempt is waste.

The two exceptions, and what they actually tell you

Tucker in 2021 and Aubrey in 2024 did stay good after hot starts. Both were elite kickers attached to strong offenses — and that's the real lesson. Knowing the offense has a little predictive value. Knowing last week's box score has none.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/04-kickers-are-noise.md

title: Just sticking to the rankings is 90% of the edge
hook: The biggest edge in our family league is not a clever strategy — it's simply sticking to a list.
html:
Confidence: High (the corrected result survived a rebuilt, tougher simulation — and the correction is the story)

TL;DR

The biggest edge in our family league is not a clever strategy — it's simply sticking to a list. A bot that drafts straight off consensus rankings, with zero opinions, beat the simulated family by almost 10 points of all-play. The best strategy we ever tested added about one more point. Discipline is roughly 90% of the available edge.

We got this one wrong first

The original version of this finding claimed the opposite: that list-following added nothing. The number was real, but our simulated opponents were too sharp — early versions of the family bots only wandered a few picks off the rankings. Then we measured our league's six real drafts and found the actual wander is 17 to 30 picks per round. Once the bots drafted like the real room, the conclusion flipped. We're publishing the correction because that's the whole point of doing this in public.

The numbers

All-play is the record you'd have if you played every team every week, so .500 is average.

DrafterAll-playTitles
RB-RB-RB opening.61021%
Rankings only, no opinions.59820%
Simulated family.5018%

Read it in two steps: showing up with any credible list and following it is worth almost 10 points and roughly two and a half times the normal title rate. Everything after that — which positions to favor, when to take a quarterback — is a fight over the last point.

What happens when everyone else sharpens up

We also ran the test in a room of eleven disciplined opponents. There, the family-style drafter loses by about 7 points — the same edge seen from the other side. And the RB-RB-RB plan loses its advantage entirely, because that plan works by harvesting our room's habit of waiting on running backs. The only strategy that kept a real edge against sharp opponents was the one doing cold math about what each pick costs to wait on.

The slide version for draft night: the sheet beats your gut by ten points; the best strategy we've ever tested beats the sheet by one.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/03-adp-discipline-is-not-an-edge.md

title: Zero RB is advice for a league we don't play in
hook: Zero RB — deliberately skipping running backs early to load up on receivers — is the most popular "smart" strategy in fantasy content, and in our league it was the worst plan we tested: a 9.7% championship rate versus 20…
html:
Confidence: High (1,440 simulated seasons per strategy, and the result got stronger when we imported the internet's best versions)

TL;DR

Zero RB — deliberately skipping running backs early to load up on receivers — is the most popular "smart" strategy in fantasy content, and in our league it was the worst plan we tested: a 9.7% championship rate versus 20.3% for opening with three straight running backs. That's half your title odds, gone. The strategy was built for leagues where catches score points. Ours isn't one.

What we found

In the same simulation as our RB-RB-RB finding, the Zero RB team posted a .548 all-play — all-play meaning the record you'd have if you played every team every week — against .598 for the RB-first plan. A WR-heavy version failed the same way, just less badly. Zero RB's one good season was 2022, the year the big running backs all busted, which is exactly the year its thesis predicts. Even then it only tied a team drafting with no strategy at all.

Why it fails here

Zero RB needs at least one of three things to work: catches that score points, a flex spot that takes tight ends, or a waiver wire with startable running backs on it. Our league has none of them. Scoring is standard, the flex is RB/WR only, and with twelve teams the other eleven rosters hold about 66 running back spots — when a backup gets promoted, he's claimed before you wake up. The receivers you hoarded instead are the one thing the wire does keep producing.

We tested Reddit's favorites too

A league-mate pointed us to a popular Reddit study that ranked draft plans for PPR leagues (leagues that pay a point per catch). We rebuilt its four named strategies and ran them in our format. Their #1 overall plan lost to RB-RB-RB here, and the pattern across all four was simple: the more early picks a plan spends away from running backs, the worse it does in our league. Format isn't a detail — it's most of the answer.

One honest limit: the simulator tests the plan, not talent. A drafter with a genuinely great eye for receivers could beat these numbers. But the plan itself starts you in a hole, and it needs an RB-bust year just to climb back to even.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/02-zero-rb-is-a-trap.md

title: Open your draft with three straight running backs
hook: In our league, starting RB-RB-RB won the championship about 20% of the time in simulation.
html:
Confidence: High (1,440 simulated seasons, and the result survived every attack we threw at it)

TL;DR

In our league, starting RB-RB-RB won the championship about 20% of the time in simulation. A team's fair share in a 12-team league is 8.3%, so that's close to two and a half times the expected rate — and no other plan we tested came close.

What we tested

We rebuilt our family league inside a simulator: same 12 teams, same standard scoring, and computer drafters trained on our last six real drafts so the room behaves like the actual room. Then we replayed six seasons 240 times each, from every draft slot, with one test team following a fixed plan — "take running backs with your first three picks, then draft normally" — against eleven bots drafting the way our family actually drafts.

The RB-RB-RB team won 20.3% of the championships. A team that just drafted for value at every pick won 17%. Zero RB — deliberately skipping running backs early, a strategy you'll see recommended all over the internet — won 9.7%, barely better than drafting on autopilot.

Why it works

Standard scoring is brutal to running backs. The top RB scores around 19 points a game and the tenth-best around 12 — a seven-point cliff. Wide receivers fall much more gently, from about 16 to 11 over the same stretch, and decent ones keep showing up on the waiver wire all season. Good running backs are the one thing you cannot get later.

Our league also waits slightly longer on running backs than the math says it should. Three top picks spent on RBs corners the scarce position while everyone else spreads out. And a roster built on three stud RBs is a boom-or-bust shape: it wins some weeks huge, and in fantasy, championships pay for booms.

Where this could go wrong

Two honest warnings. In 2022 — the year the big running backs all got hurt or flopped — this plan was nearly the worst of the disciplined strategies, and Zero RB had its one great year. The 20% is an average, not a promise. And the edge exists because our room waits on RBs; in a league full of RB-hungry drafters the advantage mostly disappears, because the backs are gone before you can corner them. That second point is measured, not a guess — see how we test drafting skill itself.

The full write-up, with every table and how to reproduce it: findings/01-robust-rb-wins.md
